ai-at-work.title: Microsoft is openly competing with OpenAI, Anthropic more than ever
ai-at-work.excerpt: Microsoft pitched its own homegrown AI models, harnesses, and even a Mythos competitor on Wednesday, telling Wall Street it plans for continued growth.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Microsoft stopped pretending to be just OpenAI's infrastructure partner and showed off its own AI lineup to investors, signaling serious competitive intent against OpenAI and Anthropic. This matters because digital workplace teams have been betting their AI strategies on the assumption that Microsoft was primarily a distributor, not a challenger. Turns out Redmond didn't spend billions licensing and integrating AI just to be someone else's middleman, which means we're about to see some genuinely interesting product competition instead of the usual vendor theater.

ai-at-work.title: Mark Zuckerberg predicts that billions of people will have personal AI agents in five years
ai-at-work.excerpt: As Meta pours billions into AI infrastructure and agents, Zuckerberg is working to convince investors that the payoff will be worth the price.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Mark Zuckerberg is betting Meta's future on personal AI agents becoming mainstream within five years, backed by massive infrastructure spending designed to convince nervous investors that the money will eventually pay off. For workplace leaders, this matters because AI agents will inevitably reshape how knowledge work gets done, from automating routine tasks to fundamentally changing how teams collaborate and make decisions. Here's the thing though: predicting the future of consumer technology is Zuckerberg's favorite hobby, and his track record on timelines is about as reliable as your company's last digital transformation estimate.

ai-at-work.title: Microsoft logs $3.2B from Anthropic investment, but OpenAI was a mixed bag
ai-at-work.excerpt: When Microsoft reported killer fourth-quarter earnings for its fiscal 2026 year (which ended June 30), it tucked in an interesting little tidbit about how its investments in the two biggest, and compe
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Microsoft marked a $3.2 billion gain on its Anthropic investment while its OpenAI bet delivered more modest returns, showing how AI bets are finally hitting the P&L in meaningful ways. For workplace leaders, this matters because it signals which AI bets are actually panning out and where the smart money thinks the technology is headed. Honestly, watching Microsoft play both sides of the AI table like a venture capitalist while also building their own shop is peak tech strategy, and it's the kind of hedging that would make any board member nervous if they were paying attention.

ai-at-work.title: Zuckerberg says Meta’s enterprise AI opportunity extends beyond agents
ai-at-work.excerpt: On the company’s second-quarter earnings call Wednesday, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta sees a “large enterprise opportunity” spanning AI agents, APIs, compute, and internal software.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta's betting that enterprises will pay for a whole stack of AI services, not just the agent chatbots everyone's been talking about. This matters because if Meta actually pulls off integrating AI into existing enterprise workflows, every other vendor will scramble to do the same, reshaping how we build and sell digital workplace tools. That said, Zuckerberg saying Meta has an "enterprise opportunity" and Meta actually executing in enterprise are two very different things, and I've watched this movie before with mixed results.

tools-tech.title: How to remap the Windows 11 Copilot key and restore your missing Right Ctrl button
tools-tech.excerpt: Pressing the Copilot key on your laptop keyboard launches Copilot. But whether or not you use Microsoft's AI, you can remap the key to trigger a different feature.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft slapped a dedicated Copilot key on Windows 11 keyboards, and it's taking up real estate that used to hold the Right Ctrl button that plenty of people actually use. This matters because IT teams are fielding complaints from users whose muscle memory and workflows got disrupted by hardware they didn't ask for, and now they need to know how to fix it. Honestly, this is Microsoft deciding for everyone that AI is the priority, which is peak "we know what you want better than you do" energy.

tools-tech.title: 74% of workers ask AI questions instead of colleagues - with potentially serious consequences
tools-tech.excerpt: A series of studies revealed that employees are spending less time asking their coworkers for help. Here's how that tactic could backfire and how organizations need to adapt.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Three-quarters of workers are now turning to AI first instead of asking their colleagues for help. This matters because it fundamentally changes how knowledge flows through organizations, erodes the informal mentoring that actually builds expertise, and quietly kills the relationships that hold teams together. Here's the thing though: if your workplace culture was strong enough, employees wouldn't be fleeing to chatbots in the first place, so maybe treat this as a mirror rather than a problem to solve with better AI policies.

digital-culture.title: Is AI really a job killer? Some employers say they’re actually hiring more
digital-culture.excerpt: The fear that AI is killing jobs has been fueled by ongoing layoffs across corporate America, most recently at companies like Visa. Just this week, the payments giant revealed plans to shed 7% of its
digital-culture.dwp_take: Some employers are claiming they're hiring more workers despite AI adoption, contradicting the widespread narrative that automation kills jobs across industries. This matters because digital workplace leaders need accurate data on whether AI displaces or creates roles, so they can plan hiring and reskilling strategies realistically. The truth is probably boring and boring is actually the story here: AI kills some jobs, creates others, and most companies are still figuring out which is which while pretending they've got it all figured out.

digital-culture.title: Remote work, flexibility influence whether women apply for a job more than men
digital-culture.excerpt: According to a recent FlexJobs survey of 1,700 U.S. workers, women place more value on remote work, flexible schedules and work-life balance when thinking about applying for a job. Men, on the other h
digital-culture.dwp_take: A FlexJobs survey found that women prioritize remote work and flexibility when job hunting, while men focus more on compensation. This matters because it tells you how to actually attract talent, not how you think you should attract it. If you're wondering why your remote-first positions get flooded with female applicants while your high-salary office gigs don't, well, there's your answer.

digital-culture.title: 92% of wealthy Americans are changing their financial plans because of this trend—and it’s reshaping how founders exit
digital-culture.excerpt: As the average life span increases, entrepreneurs are able to run their businesses for an even longer period of time. However, this shift can make deciding when—and whether—to leave considerably harde
digital-culture.dwp_take: Wealthy Americans and business founders are factoring longer lifespans into their financial planning and exit strategies, with 92% saying longevity matters to their decisions. This matters to digital workplace pros because it means leadership transitions that were once predictable five or ten year cycles are now getting stretched out, creating longer periods of uncertainty around organizational direction and strategy. Here's the thing: if your boss is planning to stick around another 20 years instead of five, that explains why your company still uses SharePoint from 2013.

digital-culture.title: 3 deceptive indicators of leadership potential you should ignore
digital-culture.excerpt: Leadership may be humanity’s single greatest invention. Long before we developed writing, money, or artificial intelligence, we learned to solve a more fundamental problem: how to coordinate large gro
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company argues that certain common signals we use to spot future leaders, like confidence or early career success, are actually terrible predictors of who will actually lead well. This matters because digital workplace teams are constantly promoting people based on these exact wrong signals, then wondering why their new manager struggles with remote teams or delegation. After three decades, I can tell you the best leaders I've seen were the quiet ones who asked good questions and made their teams smarter, not the loudest person in the room.

industry-news.title: Jeff Bezos Says Custom Chips Could Become Amazon’s Next Major Business
industry-news.excerpt: Jeff Bezos says Amazon’s Trainium, Graviton, and other custom chips could become a major business as AWS expands its AI infrastructure. The post Jeff Bezos Says Custom Chips Could Become Amazon’s Next
industry-news.dwp_take: Amazon is betting that custom silicon for AI workloads could turn into a standalone revenue stream beyond AWS infrastructure services. This matters to digital workplace pros because it signals where compute resources will come from in the next five years, and whether you're locked into one vendor's chips or have real choice in your infrastructure stack. Bezos calling this out publicly is basically Amazon saying "we're so confident in our chips that we think we can sell them like Intel used to," which is either visionary or hubris depending on how well Trainium actually performs against Nvidia in the real world.

industry-news.title: Apple Sued After Alleged Fake Crypto Wallet App Cost Users $1.8 Million
industry-news.excerpt: Three investors allege a fake Sparrow Wallet app listed in Apple’s App Store caused approximately $1.8 million in Bitcoin losses. The post Apple Sued After Alleged Fake Crypto Wallet App Cost Users $1
industry-news.dwp_take: A counterfeit crypto wallet app made it through Apple's App Store vetting process and allegedly cost three investors $1.8 million in Bitcoin losses, prompting legal action against the company. This matters because it exposes how even major platforms struggle with app verification, which directly affects enterprise security policies and how organizations advise employees on what's safe to install. After thirty years watching tech mishaps, I'll say this: if you're telling your workforce to trust the App Store because it's "curated," you might want to rethink that security conversation.

industry-news.title: The Hidden Security Problem Holding Enterprise AI Back
industry-news.excerpt: Enterprise AI adoption is accelerating, but new research suggests identity governance is lagging behind. Here's why AI agent identities are becoming a critical security challenge. The post The Hidden
industry-news.dwp_take: Companies are rolling out AI agents without proper identity governance systems in place, creating a security blind spot that nobody's really managing yet. This matters because your AI systems are now accessing the same data and systems as your employees, except nobody's tracking what they're doing or who's responsible when something goes wrong. After three decades watching security theater, I can tell you this is the classic "move fast and break things" approach colliding with regulatory reality, and it's going to get expensive before organizations figure out they needed guardrails from day one.

industry-news.title: China’s New AI Side Hustle: Renting Out Your Face
industry-news.excerpt: Chinese AI platforms are paying people to license their faces for AI-generated videos, raising new questions about biometric identity, consent, and digital ownership. The post China’s New AI Side Hust
industry-news.dwp_take: Chinese AI platforms are now paying people to license their faces for use in AI-generated videos, essentially commodifying biometric data. This matters to digital workplace pros because employee privacy, consent frameworks, and identity protection are about to become real compliance headaches if this trend spreads globally. Here's the thing: we spent years fighting for password managers and MFA, and now workers can make beer money renting their face to deepfake factories. Fun times ahead.
